Press Release:


Education Emergency
While government commends what is said to be the best matric pass rate in recent times, many education experts have cautioned against celebrating what some describe as one of the worst education systems in the world. Closer analysis suggests that, when the very high number of school drop-outs is taken into account, the pass rate is in fact far lower than that reported. Carte Blanche investigates the complex factors eating away at South Africa’s education system.


Script:


EDUCATION EMERGENCY

PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK

PRESENTER: JOHN WEBB

EDITOR: STENETTE GROSKOPFF

BROADCAST DATE: 15 JANUARY 2017

[11 JANUARY 2017] CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: You are not a Mickey Mouse School. And we want you to believe in yourself that you are indeed a top school. Year after year we are going to be expecting nothing less from this school other than 100% pass for matric.

VO: Only a week after the announcement of the matric results of the class of 2016, the pressure for the class of 2017 to out-perform them is on.
With the re-opening of schools on Wednesday this week, Deputy President Cyril Ramaphosa visited a school in the province that faired the best.

RAMAPHOSA: The Free State to be not only no 1 in the whole country, but to break the barrier and to get 93%.

VO: The 2016 pass rate increased to 72,5%, the best it’s been in recent years. This is an achievement Basic Education Minister, Angie Motshekga is very proud of.

[4 JANUARY 2017] MINISTER: The class of 2016 has recorded the enrollment of grade 12 learners in the history of our basic education system in the country. The total number of candidates who registered for 2016, was above 828 000 learners.

JOHN LINK: There is always enormous excitement when the annual matric results are announced, in fact the occasion has almost become a theatrical event. But experts are increasingly saying that it is an unnecessary and possibly even meaningless distraction.

VO: The 828-thousand full- and part time matriculants obtained a mere 158-thousand distinctions. Of those only 8000 were for Maths and 7000 for Physical Science.
Only 21 of the almost 73% that passed, obtained exemption to apply to University.
Umalusi is the independent Council for Quality Assurance and is tasked with overseeing the standardization process.

JOHN LINK: The individual figures for various subjects can be increased or decreased by a maximum of 10%. It is standard practice internationally, but in South Africa it remains controversial, with upward adjustments in particular greeted with skepticism.

VO: Umalusi CEO, dr Mafu Rakometsi says there’s no need for doubt, because it’s done according to policy.

DR MAFU RAKUMETSI: Standardisation is as old as examinations itself in this country. It is not only used in schools, it is in Universities, it is used the world-over.

VO: Nic Spaull is an educational expert at the University of Stellenbosch.

NIC SPAULL: The aim of that process is to ensure that learners do not get disadvantaged relative to other years. So, if you have a huge drop in the Maths pass rate of 2012 compared to 2011, it could be because the test papers were so much more difficult. Umalusi then adjusts the raw marks for the year that performed much worse to make sure that they aren’t disadvantaged.

DR MAFU RAKOMETSI: When we say to a University this learner has obtained a distinction in 2016, that disctinction must compare with the distinction of 2014, 2013, 2012, so that the Universities, including the employers, know what they are receiving in their system.

VO: This year, the raw marks of 32 of the 58 subjects were adjusted – 28 upwards and 4 downwards. One of the subjects that was adjusted upwards by more than 7% to 37,22% was Mathematical Literacy. It is compulsory to either have Maths or Mathematical Literacy and there is the perception that these marks, along with others that are adjusted upwards, are done to inflate the final countrywide pass rate.

DR MAFU RAKOMETSI: At the point of standardization, we don’t know what the results of the country are going to be, we do that independent of that thought, we don’t even think about the results. We are looking at the individual subject.

VO: But the standardization of subjects aside, experts are also concerned that the pass rate of 72,5% is not a true reflection, but is in fact much lower when the number of school drop-outs is taken into account.

NIC SPAULL: I would say pass rate is about 56%, the real matric pass rate. If you look at the traditional cohort, about 56% of them will reach matric and pass matric.

VO: In 2014, there were 1,1 million learners in Grade 10. Only 45% of them wrote matric in 2016.

NIC SPAULL: Historically South Africa has a disproportionately high number of students that reach upper high school, but historically we also have a lower number that actually graduate.

VO: But Education spokesperson, Elijah Mahlanga says it’s absurd to calculate the 2016 matric pass rate according to the number of students who were in grade 10 in 2014.

ELIJAH MAHLANGA: We count those that wrote the examination and we base the percentage on those that wrote the examination. Remember, there are many reasons for drop-out – other are due to substance abuse, others get arrested, others leave school due to frustration in the difficulty of the curriculum, so there is a variety of reasons.

JOHN LINK: Inevitably, most of those who don’t complete their schooling end up joining the more than 30% of people in this country who are unemployed. Now, to overcome that problem, the Department of Education has come up with a unique, but controversial solution.

VO: The solution is called The Policy on Progression. It was implemented in 2013 and states that a learner cannot repeat a grade more than once in a phase of three years. If the learner fails a grade for the second time, he or she is automatically progressed to the next grade.

NIC SPAULL: From 2013, 2014 to 2015 we saw a huge decline in the raw marks, particularly in subjects such as Maths and Umalusi interpreted this as that the papers were getting much more difficult. But a much more plausible explanation that myself and other commentators and critics have put forward is that we included 120 000 weaker students in 2015 that were not there in 2013.

VO: Although it’s a contentious issue, holding back students is not necessarily a better option, says dr Lee Ruzsnyak (Rizz-nee-yak), an Educational Expert at WITS University.

DR LEE RUZSNYAK: When children repeat a year, but the teacher does exactly what was done the previous year, there is actually no substantial intervention. So, for retention to have any value at all, the teaching and the learning has to improve, it can’t just be same old, same old and the child with those same gaps will continue with the same gaps. It is not addressing anything.

ELIJAH: We are progressing learners who are not making it, so that they can stay in the education system, that is how we are trying to solve the drop-out rate. So, as you attack the progression policy, do think about those learners – they would be in the streets and you would be coming to us and say: “What are you doing about the drop-out rate?” So, this is what we are doing. We are supporting them, we are making sure that we give them extra tuition time.

MAFU RAKUMETSI: The question arises – what do you do with those kids? Those kids have to be taken through the schooling system, we have to make them viable in terms of them being functional citizens fending for their families. So, it is something we have to commend the department for.

MINISTER: We thank all provinces for the extra support they have given to these learners because some of them could have fallen through the cracks of the system due to continuous repetition and others could have dropped out from the schooling system.

VO: 109 400 progressed learners wrote the matric exam this year.
Of those learners, sixty-seven percent wrote the full exam. Twenty-seven percent of them passed.
The remaining 33% of the progressed learners only wrote three subjects last year and will conclude the exam in June.

JOHN LINK: We tend to judge the health of our education system on how many matrics passed their final exams, but that can often give a skewed picture. In fact, it is on primary school, the so-called foundation phase that we should be focusing and sadly there, the picture isn’t quite as rosy.

LEE RUZSNYAK: In an ideal world where everything is working the way it is, in grades 1, 2 and 3 you learn to read. And grade 4, 5 and onwards, there is an adjustment, a shift from learning to read, to reading to learn and engaging with texts and analyzing texts and that’s the basis for any kind of literacy.

NIC SPAULL: The fact that children are not getting a solid foundation in primary school, in reading and in mathematics, in numeracy and literacy, the fact that we have more than half of our students that aren’t learning to read for meaning by grade 4, that is the real cause of our repetition problem, the fact that all of these students are dropping out is underpinned by the fact that they aren’t acquiring skills that are prepping them for success.

ELIJAH: The matric focus made people to only look at the prevalence of high school and we neglected the primary school, so we are saying now let’s go back there and look at what is happening, because if you are seeing a good performance at foundation phase at the primary school, then you are likely to see same at high school, secondary school level.

VO: And with the focus squarely on education at the beginning of the new school year, critics site the World Economic Forum’s annual competitiveness survey which ranked South Africa at 126 out of 138 on the quality of basic education. Various studies also consistently rank Maths and Science education in the country as well below par.

NIC SPAULL: Even if you take the 75 odd countries that the OECD looks at, South Africa comes 74 of roughly 75 countries which is extremely low, but there are more than 75 countries in the world, so it is rarely saying that we are bottom of the class of those that actually measure their learning. What they didn’t emphasize is that South Africa was the fastest improving country over the last 12 years. So, the way that I describe it is our education system is dire, but it is improving.

DR MAFU RAKUMETSI: For us to say it is all doom and gloom in this country is not true, it cannot be true. Yes, there are weaknesses, but you have to raise those weaknesses being careful not to discourage even the learners who have passed matric last year.

PROMOS

PROMO 3: 10”

VO: The Education Department is trumpeting what it says is the best matric pass rate in recent years, but experts suggest the true figure is far lower than 72,5%.

PROMO 1: 15”

CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: You are not a Mickey Mouse School.

VO: Only a week after the announcement of the 2016-matric results, the pressure for the 2017-class to out-perform them is on.
But is the emphasis of our education system not perhaps misplaced?


PROMO 2: 15”

VO: South Africa’s education system is faced with a myriad of challenges – But is there a future for learners?

NIC SPAULL: The way I see it, is that the education system is dire, but it is improving.
